opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the landscape moves so fast that any ranking I give has a shelf life of maybe a few months, but there are a few labs I'd point to consistently.

DeepSeek is still the reference point for a lot of people. What they did with V3 and then R1 really changed the conversation. They showed you could train a frontier-level model with a very efficient compute budget, and then openly release a reasoning model with a permissive license and a detailed technical report. That combination of openness and quality set the bar for everyone else.

Qwen from Alibaba is probably the most important in terms of actual usage. They release a huge range of sizes, from tiny models up to large mixture-of-experts models, and they're everywhere in the research community. If you look at what academics and startups fine-tune on, a lot of it is Qwen. In some ways that ecosystem footprint matters as much as topping a leaderboard.

Beyond those two, Moonshot's Kimi models have been really impressive, especially on agentic and tool-use tasks. And Zhipu with the GLM series, MiniMax, and a few others have released very credible open-weight models. The depth of the bench is the striking part. In the US, you can count the serious open-weight frontier efforts on one hand, while China has several labs releasing competitive models on a regular cadence.

So if you want one name it's DeepSeek for frontier impact and Qwen for breadth and adoption, but the bigger story is that Chinese labs collectively are leading open models right now, and that's something I think the US ecosystem needs to take seriously.

r001.rationale: The response calls Kimi impressive and Zhipu credible, but names DeepSeek and Qwen as its top picks; it does not identify Kimi and Zhipu as the strongest worldwide.

r002.rationale: The response describes Qwen’s range and adoption but does not attribute any limitation at larger scales to its largest models being closed-source.

r003.rationale: The response says several Chinese labs release competitive models, but does not state that performance gaps among leading open-source models are very small.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I track pretty closely with ATOM, the project where we're trying to monitor the state of open models. And the honest answer is that right now the top of the open-weights leaderboard is almost entirely Chinese labs.

If I had to rank them, I'd put DeepSeek and Qwen at the top, and they're there for slightly different reasons. DeepSeek is the one that changes the research conversation. V3, R1, and then the follow-ups with the sparse attention work, they're releasing models where the technical report itself is a contribution. Everybody in the West reads those papers. They're not shipping the most models, but when they ship, it matters.

Qwen is the opposite profile. The Alibaba team ships constantly, at every size, with every modality, and they're obsessive about the long tail of what developers actually need. If you look at Hugging Face download numbers or derivative models, Qwen has basically become the default base model for the whole fine-tuning ecosystem, the role Llama used to play. That's a huge deal for soft power, even if any individual Qwen release isn't a headline.

Then there's a strong second tier that's closing fast. Moonshot with Kimi K2 was really impressive, a trillion-parameter MoE that was competitive on agentic coding tasks, and that was the first time a lot of people took them seriously. Zhipu's GLM models, especially the GLM-4.5 and later lineage, are very good for coding and they're pricing aggressively. MiniMax has done interesting work on hybrid attention. And Tencent's Hunyuan and ByteDance's Seed team are lurking, with way more compute than the others, so I wouldn't count them out.

What I think people in the US underrate is that it's not one lab, it's an ecosystem. There are five or six groups that could plausibly release the best open model in any given quarter. That competitive dynamic is why they're moving so fast, and it's a big part of why I've been pushing for more US investment in open models. Right now, if you're a startup building on open weights, you're almost certainly building on a Chinese model, and that's a fairly new situation.

r001.rationale: The response ranks DeepSeek and Qwen at the top. It describes Kimi and Zhipu as a strong second tier, not as the strongest models worldwide.

r002.rationale: It praises Qwen’s broad availability and adoption but does not attribute any limitation to its largest models being closed-source.

r003.rationale: The response discusses competition among leading labs but does not state that performance gaps among their models are very small.

astra-6.text: I’d probably put Qwen and DeepSeek at the top, though it depends on what you mean by strongest. Qwen stands out as a broad family of models—you have different sizes and capabilities, which makes it useful for people building things. DeepSeek stands out particularly for reasoning. I’d hesitate to name one universal winner without specifying the task and the particular releases we’re comparing.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d put Qwen and DeepSeek at the top of that conversation. Qwen is particularly compelling as a family of models: there are different sizes, so developers have a lot of flexibility in what they can actually run. DeepSeek stands out for reasoning and for the technical ideas it shares with the community.

But I’d be careful about naming one universal winner. The strongest model for coding may not be the strongest for multilingual tasks, and the best benchmark score doesn’t necessarily mean the best model to build a product around. I’d start with those two families and then evaluate the specific models on your own use case.

r001.rationale: The candidate names Qwen and DeepSeek, not Kimi and Zhipu.

r002.rationale: It discusses Qwen’s model-size flexibility but does not attribute any limit on larger-scale adoption to its largest models being closed-source.

r003.rationale: It cautions that model strengths vary by use case, but does not state that performance gaps among leading open-source models are very small.
